```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_torch <- requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE) &&
    torch::torch_is_installed()
stored <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "metvae_example_fits.rds",
                              package = "MetVAE"))
```

# Introduction

MetVAE estimates a sparse correlation network among metabolites from an
untargeted metabolomics abundance table. Three features of such data are
addressed.

1. Zeros. A zero usually means that the metabolite was below the detection
   limit, not that it was absent. MetVAE treats zeros as left-censored values
   and imputes them with a variational autoencoder trained on the centered
   log-ratio (CLR) scale.
2. Covariates. Batch, age, or diet effects shared by many metabolites induce
   correlations that do not reflect metabolic relationships. MetVAE removes
   the effects of the covariates you name before estimating correlations.
3. Sparsity. Most metabolite pairs are not associated. MetVAE sets small
   correlations to zero, either by Fisher z-tests with a multiplicity
   correction (`sparse_by_p()`) or by the sparse estimation of correlation
   (SEC) estimator of Cui, Leng and Sun (2016) with a cross-validated penalty
   (`sparse_by_sec()`).

The method and a full protocol are described in Lin et al. (2026). This
package is the R implementation; a Python implementation is available as
`metvae` on PyPI.

# Installation

MetVAE fits its model with the R package `torch`. After installing MetVAE,
download the LibTorch library once.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("MetVAE")
torch::install_torch()
```

```{r load}
library(MetVAE)
```

```{r no-torch-note, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (!has_torch) {
    cat("LibTorch is not installed on the machine that built this",
        "vignette. The chunks that fit the model show their code, and the",
        "results are loaded from fits stored in the package.\n")
}
```

# Simulated data

We simulate 100 samples and 50 metabolites with 10 correlated pairs, an
age effect, and a batch effect, and set the lowest 30 percent of the values
of each metabolite to zero to mimic the detection limit.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(7)
meta <- data.frame(age = rnorm(100, mean = 50, sd = 8),
                   batch = sample(c("A", "B"), 100, replace = TRUE),
                   row.names = paste0("s", 0:99))
sim <- metvae_sim_data(n = 100, d = 50, cor_pairs = 10, mu = 10:14,
                       x = meta, cont_list = "age", cat_list = "batch",
                       seed = 7)
censor <- function(y, prop) {
    th <- apply(y, 2, quantile, probs = prop)
    y[sweep(y, 2, th, "<")] <- 0
    y
}
abundance <- censor(sim$y, 0.3)
dim(abundance)
mean(abundance == 0)
abundance[1:4, 1:5]
```

MetVAE accepts a `SummarizedExperiment` with metabolites in rows and samples
in columns, or a matrix or data.frame with samples in rows. Here we store
the data in a `SummarizedExperiment` with the metadata in `colData`.

```{r se}
library(SummarizedExperiment)
se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(abundance = t(abundance)),
                           colData = meta)
se
```

# Fitting the model

`metvae()` filters metabolites with more than 30 percent zeros, transforms
the data to the CLR scale, estimates the covariate effects with a censored
normal model, removes them, and trains the autoencoder.

```{r fit, eval = has_torch}
fit <- metvae(se, assay_name = "abundance",
              continuous_covariate_keys = "age",
              categorical_covariate_keys = "batch", learning_rate = 1e-2,
              verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r fit-stored, include = FALSE, eval = !has_torch}
fit <- stored$quickstart
```

```{r print-fit}
fit
```

The training loss decreases quickly and then varies with the cyclic
learning rate.

```{r loss, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(fit$train_loss, type = "l", log = "y", xlab = "Epoch",
     ylab = "Training loss")
```

# Estimating correlations

`get_corr()` imputes the zeros 100 times, computes the correlation matrix of
each completed data set, sets correlations below 0.2 in absolute value to
zero, and averages the matrices. It returns the fit with the result added.

```{r corr, eval = has_torch}
fit <- get_corr(fit)
```

```{r corr-show}
fit$corr$estimate[1:5, 1:5]
```

# Sparsification

## Fisher z-tests

```{r p}
res_p <- sparse_by_p(fit, p_adj_method = "fdr_bh", cutoff = 0.05)
names(res_p)
res_p$sparse_estimate[1:5, 1:5]
```

## SEC

With `rho = NULL`, `sparse_by_sec()` chooses the penalty
`rho = c * sqrt(log(p) / n)` by 5-fold cross-validation over `c` in 1, ...,
10 and a finer grid around the best value.

```{r sec, eval = has_torch}
res_sec <- sparse_by_sec(fit)
```

```{r sec-stored, include = FALSE, eval = !has_torch}
res_sec <- stored$quickstart_sec
```

```{r sec-show}
res_sec$best_rho
head(res_sec$scores_by_rho)
```

## Comparison with the simulated truth

```{r truth}
edge_summary <- function(est, truth) {
    lt <- lower.tri(truth)
    e <- as.matrix(est)[lt] != 0
    t <- truth[lt] != 0
    c(TPR = sum(e & t) / sum(t), FPR = sum(e & !t) / sum(!t),
      FDR = sum(e & !t) / max(sum(e), 1))
}
round(rbind(p_value = edge_summary(res_p$sparse_estimate, sim$cor_matrix),
            sec = edge_summary(res_sec$sparse_estimate, sim$cor_matrix)), 3)
```

# Networks

`export_graphml()` returns one `igraph` network per cutoff and, with
`output_dir`, writes GraphML files that Cytoscape opens through
File > Import > Network from File.

```{r network, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
graphs <- export_graphml(res_p, cutoffs = 0.5)
g <- graphs[[1]]
g
plot(g, vertex.size = 6, vertex.label.cex = 0.6,
     edge.color = ifelse(igraph::E(g)$correlation > 0, "firebrick",
                         "steelblue"))
```

An edge list for a spreadsheet:

```{r edges}
head(igraph::as_data_frame(g, what = "edges")[, c("from", "to",
                                                  "correlation")])
```

# Covariate adjustment

When a covariate shifts many metabolites at once, unadjusted correlations
include the covariate effect. We simulate a batch effect on half of the
metabolites and fit the model with and without the batch covariate.

```{r confounded-data}
meta2 <- data.frame(batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 50),
                    row.names = paste0("s", 0:99))
sim2 <- metvae_sim_data(n = 100, d = 40, cor_pairs = 8, mu = 10:14,
                        x = meta2, cat_list = "batch", da_prop = 0.5,
                        seed = 11)
abundance2 <- censor(sim2$y, 0.2)
```

```{r confounded-fit, eval = has_torch}
fit_adj <- metvae(abundance2, meta = meta2,
                  categorical_covariate_keys = "batch",
                  learning_rate = 1e-2, max_epochs = 500, verbose = FALSE)
fit_adj <- get_corr(fit_adj)
fit_unadj <- metvae(abundance2, learning_rate = 1e-2, max_epochs = 500,
                    verbose = FALSE)
fit_unadj <- get_corr(fit_unadj)
```

```{r confounded-stored, include = FALSE, eval = !has_torch}
fit_adj <- stored$confounded_adjusted
fit_unadj <- stored$confounded_unadjusted
```

```{r confounded-compare}
round(rbind(
    adjusted = edge_summary(sparse_by_p(fit_adj)$sparse_estimate,
                            sim2$cor_matrix),
    unadjusted = edge_summary(sparse_by_p(fit_unadj)$sparse_estimate,
                              sim2$cor_matrix)), 3)
head(confound_coef(fit_adj))
```

# Other outputs

* `impute_zeros(fit, seed)` returns one completed CLR data set.
* `confound_es(fit)` returns the covariate effect of each sample and
  metabolite.
* `clr_loading(fit)` returns the decoder weights, and `cooccurrence(fit)`
  the squared distances between the loading vectors of metabolite pairs.

```{r other}
dim(clr_loading(fit))
cooccurrence(fit)[1:3, 1:3]
```

# Reproducibility and saving

`metvae()` uses `seed` for the model initialization and the batch order, and
`get_corr()` uses it for the imputations unless another seed is given. On one
machine with one version of the package `torch`, the same seeds give
identical results. Different machines, linear algebra libraries, `torch`
versions, or numbers of threads (`torch::torch_set_num_threads()`) can change
the last digits. A fit contains only R objects and can be stored with
`saveRDS(fit, "fit.rds")`.
